content.title: Signal Blocks Screenshots to Thwart AI Agents
content.introduction: Signal has introduced an optional setting that prevents screenshots on supported mobile devices, aiming to stop built‑in AI agents from reading message content. This move marks a notable privacy‑focused response to the growing integration of AI features in messaging apps.

articles.headline: Signal adds optional screenshot block to curb AI agents
articles.summary: Signal now offers a setting that blocks screenshots on supported mobile platforms to stop built‑in AI agents from reading message content.
paragraphs: The encrypted‑messaging app has introduced a new toggle that, when enabled, prevents the operating system from capturing screenshots of the Signal UI. This measure targets the latest AI agents embedded in iOS and Android that can otherwise harvest visible text for processing. Users can turn the protection off, but doing so re‑exposes their chats to those agents and nullifies Signal’s privacy guarantee.

Signal notes the feature does not cover all Android devices and cannot block Siri on macOS because Apple provides no reliable screenshot‑blocking API. For macOS 27 users, the only current mitigation is to add Signal to the Excluded Apps list under System Settings → Siri.
The company calls on Apple, Google and Microsoft to expose clear APIs for developers to block AI‑driven data capture, warning that existing work‑arounds leave gaps in protection.
articles.implication: Developers and privacy‑focused users must treat the screenshot block as a partial safeguard that works only on certain platforms and requires manual activation, while still lobbying OS vendors for proper API support.

articles.headline: Vercel earns ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI management certification
articles.summary: Vercel’s AI platform, including AI Gateway and Vercel Agent, is now certified under the international AI management standard, giving customers a formally audited foundation.
paragraphs: The certification, valid for three years with annual surveillance, confirms that Vercel’s design, build, operation and governance processes for its AI services meet ISO/IEC 42001:2023 requirements. The audit highlights a shared‑responsibility model, where Vercel documents its obligations and customers retain responsibility for their own AI use cases.
articles.implication: Enterprises can rely on Vercel’s AI products as a pre‑audited component, reducing the effort needed to demonstrate compliance with AI governance standards in their own deployments.

articles.headline: Google adds Duplex calling to Gemini Tasks
articles.summary: Google’s Gemini app now includes the Duplex voice‑calling feature, letting the personal AI place calls to businesses on a user’s behalf.
paragraphs: The new capability, announced on 20 Nov 2026, extends the decade‑old Duplex system into the Gemini Tasks experience. It builds on a hybrid stack that pairs generative Gemini models with deterministic state tracking and policy guardrails, ensuring calls remain predictable and compliant. The feature is limited to the Gemini Tasks app and relies on the existing Gemini foundation model; no separate API or SDK is provided for third‑party integration.
articles.implication: Developers building on Gemini can now rely on built‑in voice‑calling for user‑initiated tasks, but must stay within the Gemini Tasks environment to access it.

articles.headline: Vercel Functions add 20 MiB request‑body limit in public beta
articles.summary: Vercel now lets Functions on Node.js, Python, and Bun accept bodies up to 20 MiB when the VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY flag is enabled.
paragraphs: The opt‑in requires the project’s functions to run with the 4 GB performance memory setting; Edge runtime functions remain capped at 4.5 MiB and will return 413 on larger payloads. Middleware continues to see headers but not the body, so any logic that depends on the request body must be moved into the function itself. Vercel advises reading the body promptly to avoid back‑pressure and memory spikes.
articles.implication: Projects that need larger uploads must switch to a supported runtime and enable the flag, but they lose body‑aware middleware and must manage memory carefully.

articles.headline: Cloudflare WAF adds rules to block ruby2shell exploit
articles.summary: Cloudflare introduced two managed‑ruleset entries that block the newly disclosed ruby2shell heap overflow (CVE‑2026‑132825) for all customers.
paragraphs: The new rules target the Ruby string‑case conversion bug that overflows a buffer when handling the German sharp‑s (ß) and also cover the related GHSA‑87fm‑7w84‑j2px integer overflow. Cloudflare notes that the WAF is a compensating control; the only complete mitigation is upgrading Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13, or 4.0.10.
articles.implication: Customers receive immediate protection via Cloudflare’s free managed ruleset, but must still schedule Ruby upgrades to fully eliminate the vulnerability.

articles.headline: Fastify reply‑from plugin fixes request‑smuggling bug
articles.summary: Fastify’s @fastify/reply-from 12.9.1 patches a request‑smuggling flaw that let unauthenticated clients inject arbitrary upstream requests.
paragraphs: Versions prior to 12.9.1 forward a client’s Content‑Length even when no body is sent, causing keep‑alive sockets to retain unread bytes; a GET, HEAD or TRACE with a body (or a falsy JSON payload) can then make the upstream read the next request as part of the previous one. The update forces the plugin to forward any parsed body and resets an inherited Content‑Length to 0 when no body is written, eliminating the mismatch. Using the default undici transport avoids the issue entirely.
articles.implication: Deploying 12.9.1 or switching to undici prevents attackers from bypassing Fastify’s routing and authentication via smuggled requests.

lessons.title: Why blocking screenshots limits AI agents but is not a complete solution
paragraphs: Signal’s optional setting stops the operating system from capturing screenshots of the Signal interface on platforms that provide a screenshot‑blocking API. This prevents AI agents that rely on reading on‑screen content from obtaining a visual copy of messages.

The feature works on many iOS and Android devices, but it does not apply to all Android models and is unavailable on macOS because Apple does not expose a reliable screenshot‑blocking API. Consequently, the toggle offers protection only where the OS supports it and must be turned on manually.
lessons.example: When a user enables the screenshot‑blocking toggle on a supported Android phone, attempts by any app—including a built‑in AI assistant—to capture the screen are blocked by the operating system, so the assistant cannot obtain an image of the Signal conversation.
lessons.takeaway: Blocking screenshots removes a straightforward way for AI agents to read on‑screen messages, but it is a partial safeguard that depends on OS support and manual activation; developers and users should continue to advocate for broader, documented protections.

quiz.prompt: What is the primary reason that blocking screenshots does not provide complete protection against AI agents?
options: Because the feature must be manually enabled by the user
Because AI agents can still read messages directly from the network
Because the OS may not support a screenshot‑blocking API on all devices
Because the blocked screenshots are stored in a cloud backup
quiz.explanation: The lesson explains that the protection only works where the operating system provides a screenshot‑blocking API, and many Android models and macOS lack such support, making the safeguard partial.

quiz.prompt: On which platforms is the Signal screenshot‑blocking toggle unavailable according to the lesson?
options: iOS devices that lack a screenshot‑blocking API
quiz.explanation: The lesson states that the toggle is unavailable on macOS because Apple does not expose a reliable screenshot‑blocking API.

quiz.prompt: Which condition must be met for the screenshot‑blocking feature to stop an AI assistant from capturing a Signal conversation?
options: The device must be running a supported OS version with the API and the toggle must be turned on
The AI assistant must be granted explicit permission to access the screen
Signal must be running in a sandboxed environment
The user must disable all background apps
quiz.explanation: The lesson notes that the feature works only where the OS supports the screenshot‑blocking API and only when the user manually enables the toggle.

segments.title: Signal adds optional screenshot block
segments.text:
Hello everyone, and welcome to Daywire. Let's make sense of the tech news. It's November twenty one, two thousand twenty six.

We begin with our lead story. Signal now lets you flip a switch that stops your phone from taking screenshots of the app. The idea is to keep the newest AI assistants on iOS and Android from reading what you type. It works on supported mobile devices, but Android coverage is spotty and it can’t stop Siri on macOS because Apple doesn’t offer a blocking API. So, it’s a handy extra layer if you enable it, but it’s not a blanket shield – you still need the OS makers to give developers proper tools.
The takeaway? Turn it on where it works, but don’t count on it to protect every chat.

segments.title: Vercel AI Platform Gains ISO Management Certification
segments.text: Next on the bulletin. Vercel’s AI platform just earned ISO slash IEC four two zero zero one two thousand twenty three certification. That means its AI Gateway and Vercel Agent have been audited and found to follow the international AI management standard for design, build, operation and governance. The audit also notes a shared‑responsibility model – Vercel documents its part, but customers still own how they use the AI. Here’s why that matters: enterprises can now lean on Vercel’s pre‑audited services to cut down the work needed for their own AI governance compliance, though they still have to manage their own use cases.

segments.title: Google adds Duplex calls to Gemini Tasks
segments.text: Turning to our next story. Google adds Duplex calling to Gemini Tasks. The feature, announced on 20 Nov 2026, folds the decade‑old Duplex voice‑calling system into the Gemini Tasks app, pairing generative Gemini models with deterministic state tracking and policy guardrails. It means the personal AI can place calls to businesses for you, but only inside the Gemini Tasks environment – there’s no separate API or SDK for third‑party use. Here’s why that matters: developers get built‑in voice calling, yet they must stay within Gemini Tasks to access it.

segments.title: Vercel Functions raise request body limit to twenty mebibytes
segments.text:
Next on the bulletin. Vercel Functions are now offering a twenty mebibytes request‑body ceiling in public beta. To unlock it you flip the VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY flag and run your functions with the four gigabytes performance memory setting. Edge runtime functions stay capped at four point five mebibytes and will return a four one three if you exceed that, and middleware will only see headers, not the body. Vercel advises reading the body right away to keep memory spikes in check.

The practical upshot? If you need bigger uploads you can switch runtimes and enable the flag, but you’ll lose body‑aware middleware and must watch your memory usage closely.

segments.title: Cloudflare blocks ruby2shell exploit with new WAF rules
segments.text:
And finally, our last story. Cloudflare has added two managed‑ruleset entries that stop the ruby2shell heap overflow from slipping through its web application firewall.

The rules target the Ruby string‑case conversion bug that overflows a buffer on the German sharp‑s and also catch a related integer overflow. The immediate effect is that traffic is filtered at the edge, but the only way to fully eliminate the flaw is to upgrade Ruby to version three point three point fourteen, three point four point thirteen, or four point zero point ten.

Plan those Ruby upgrades soon.

And that's your Daywire briefing. You'll find the full stories and sources in today's newspaper. Thanks for listening. Take care, everyone.
